title: transient-dns-cname-cache-probe-notes
content:
Summary:
- Intermittent failures on private deployment when resolving customer-hosted model endpoints (tls: certificate name mismatch, sometimes connects fine). Suspect stale CNAME resolution cached on peered VPC NAT/forwarder path.

What I observed (high level):
- App in customer VPC A -> peered to Redwood VPC B via VPC peering (transit via vendor virtual appliance).
- Requests to api.customer-models.example.com occasionally resolve to old-cname.edge-old.example.net instead of edge-new.example.net. Old CNAME maps to decommissioned egress IP ranges (NAT gateway removed last month).
- Result: TCP established but TLS SNI mismatches against ip-based cert (RST later), or TLS handshake fails with "certificate common name xyz does not match".
- Failures are bursty and correlate with short traffic spikes and NAT failover events.

Timeline + quick notes:
- 2025-01-10 09:18: spike of 5xxes from customer, repeated curl failures shown below.
- 2025-01-10 09:20: ran dns probe from pod (see commands).
- 2025-01-10 09:34: vendor appliance logs show cached answer for cname for ~8m after their internal glue update.

Commands I ran (raw-ish):
- from failing pod (busybox):
  # busybox nslookup api.customer-models.example.com 8.8.8.8
  Server: 8.8.8.8
  Address: 8.8.8.8:53

  Name: api.customer-models.example.com
  Address 1: 10.11.12.13 (internal LB - expected)

- using dig + trace + tcpdump on node:
  $ dig +trace api.customer-models.example.com @10.0.0.2 +noall +answer
  api.customer-models.example.com. 300 IN CNAME edge-old.example.net.
  edge-old.example.net. 300 IN A 192.0.2.34

  (later after flushing cache on appliance)
  api.customer-models.example.com. 300 IN CNAME edge-new.example.net.
  edge-new.example.net. 60 IN A 198.51.100.45

- curl verbose (when failing):
  $ curl -v --resolve api.customer-models.example.com:443:192.0.2.34 https://api.customer-models.example.com/health
  * Connected to 192.0.2.34 (192.0.2.34) port 443 (#0)
  * ALPN, offering h2
  * TLSv1.3 (INTERNAL), Cipher ...
  * Server certificate:
    subject: CN=edge-new.example.net
    start date: Jan 1 00:00:00 2025 GMT
  * TLS alert, server closed connection
  curl: (56) Received reset or unexpected EOF

- tcpdump during failure window (node):
  09:19:11.123 IP pod-xxx.12345 > 192.0.2.34.443: Flags [S], seq 12345
  09:19:11.456 IP 192.0.2.34.443 > pod-xxx.12345: Flags [S.], seq 54321, ack 12346
  09:19:11.789 IP 192.0.2.34.443 > pod-xxx.12345: Flags [RST]

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Vendor peering appliance has an aggressive internal DNS cache for CNAME chains and did not pick up the customer's glue change quickly -> some nodes resolve old edge-old IPs. (most likely)
2) Intermediate NAT / egress device reused an old connection tracking entry mapping to the removed NAT IP -> packets routed to wrong host and TLS fails.
3) Split-horizon DNS: internal resolver returns edge-old for certain subnets due to ACLs; occasional routing path uses that subnet.
4) Client-side pod caching or node nscd misconfigured (less likely since dig +trace on node showed CNAME).

Experiments run and outcomes:
- Flushed vendor appliance DNS cache (vendor support): failure rate dropped to near zero for ~12m, then a few residual failures.
- Added an explicit iptables rule to drop traffic to 192.0.2.0/24 on the node and watched failover -> requests retried and started resolving to edge-new (evidence that route + cached DNS both matter).
- Tested TTL override by changing stub resolver to prefer shorter TTLs (not doable in prod).
- Instrumented pod to log resolved IP + stacktrace on handshake failure (added quick env var DEBUG_DNS_RESOLVE=1).

Short playbook (quick steps to triage next time):
1) from failing pod: curl -v --resolve HOST:443:RESOLVED_IP to reproduce and capture cert subject.
2) on node: dig +trace HOST @node-resolver ; tcpdump -w /tmp/host-traffic.pcap port 443 and capture 30s around event.
3) query vendor appliance cache API (/cache/lookup?name=) if available and record timestamps.
4) if appliance shows stale entry, escalate to vendor with cache key + TTL + sample pcap + dig output.
5) temporary mitigations: add iptables drop for decommissioned IP range or route blackhole, or change egress mapping to use different NAT pool.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we add an automated health check that resolves host -> verify cert CN matches expected and failover to alternative path? (Rosa to prototype)
- Should we require vendors to implement DNS cache invalidation webhook for config updates? (raise in infra vendor review)
- Check if Kubernetes node-local resolver (systemd-resolved / nscd) is contributing to sticky answers; test with node-level cache flush script.

Notes to self / bits: 
- Pay attention to CNAME chains longer than 1, those are where appliance caches tend to be sticky.
- Collect resolver logs from both sides of peering when next incident occurs.

Useful commands snippet to keep handy:
- dig +trace api.customer-models.example.com @10.0.0.2 +noall +answer
- curl -v --resolve api.customer-models.example.com:443:<ip> https://api.customer-models.example.com/health
- sudo tcpdump -i any host <ip> and port 443 -w /tmp/trace.pcap
- ssh to vendor appliance -> show dns cache api (if they expose it)

Attachments to create: pcap samples, vendor cache dump, dig traces.

Last quick checklist before handing to support: dns trace, pcap, sample curl output, timeline, node id, pod id, affected customer endpoints.

End of scratchpad.
